Same Answer, Different Confidence:
Protocol Sensitivity in Measuring LLM Confidence

Hankyeol Kim    Pilsung Kang* Affiliation: Seoul National University Email: {hankyeol,pilsung_kang}@snu.ac.kr Affiliation: *Corresponding author
Abstract

Large language models (LLM) can state their confidence in an answer (verbalized confidence), or the confidence can be read from the probability of the answer’s tokens (token confidence). Comparisons of the two ask which is better calibrated, but the token probability of an answer depends on the text that precedes it. Across five open LLMs and four question-answering datasets, we fix each answer, its verbalized confidence, and its correctness label, and vary how each score is measured. The scores themselves change with the protocol, and so does the comparison between them. Changing the context in which the token probability is read shifts the gap between the two scores by about the size of the gap itself (.287.287 vs. .304.304 in expected calibration error, ECE; .189.189 vs. .145.145 in AUROC). The 95% interval of the shift excludes zero in 19 and 17 of the 20 settings, and under AUROC the shift has the same sign in all of them, so the context changes how answers are ranked. The better score flips in 8 settings under each metric, counting only flips that the intervals support, and the shift also appears in four larger models of up to 72B parameters. Most of the shift appears with changes to the instruction, not to the position of the answer. Other measurement choices also matter, and stated confidence depends on how a supplied answer is written. We turn these results into a reporting checklist for LLM confidence and its comparisons.

1 Introduction

A language model’s confidence in an answer can be measured in two ways. The model can state a probability in words, or we can compute the probability of the answer’s tokens under the model. Studies that compare these verbalized and token scores usually ask which of the two methods is better calibrated, and they reach different conclusions (Tian et al., 2023; Ni et al., 2024).

The token score of an answer depends on the text that precedes it: the same answer gets a different token score after a bare question than after the prompt that asked the model for its answer and its confidence. Prior work has studied how each score changes with the prompt or the metric (§2.2), but less is known about how such choices change which of the two scores looks better.

Token probabilities are known to vary with the prompt (Zhao et al., 2021). However, it remains unclear how much each score changes with the measurement protocol, and whether the change is large enough to alter the conclusion of a comparison between them. To measure this, we fix each model’s answer, its verbalized score, and its correctness label, and vary the remaining measurement choices (Figure 1). Most importantly, we read the token score of the same answer in three contexts. We also vary how token probabilities are combined, the correctness rule, and the estimator of expected calibration error (ECE; §3.5), and we probe the verbalized score with answers that we supply. We test five open instruction-tuned models on four question-answering datasets, which gives 20 settings, and check four larger models of up to 72B parameters.

Changing the context from a bare question to the prompt that produced the answer changes the gap between the two scores by about as much as the gap itself. Under ECE, the gap moves by .287.287 on average, against a bare-context gap of .304.304; under AUROC, which measures how well a score ranks right answers above wrong ones, it moves by .189.189, against .145.145. Under AUROC, the shift goes the same way in all 20 settings, so the context changes the order of the answers, not only the scale of the scores. We show this shift also appears in the larger models. Most of the shift appears when we change the instruction in the prompt, not where the answer begins. As a result, two prompts that both omit a confidence request can still lead to different conclusions. Other choices, such as the correctness rule and the way token probabilities are combined, also change the gap, in some settings enough to change which score looks better. On the verbalized side, stated confidence for a supplied answer changes with how a correct answer is written, barely separates a correct answer from a plausible wrong one, and leans toward the model’s own wrong answers.

Our contributions are as follows:

  • •

    We study the sensitivity and robustness of LLM confidence across measurement choices, a prompt ablation, and supplied answers (§4).

  • •

    Using a design that fixes the answer and its label, we show that the context in which the token score is read changes the comparison between verbalized and token confidence about as much as the gap itself (§3, §4.1).

  • •

    We identify the factors that matter most for measuring LLM confidence and summarize them as a reporting checklist (Table 5).

2 Related Work

2.1 Verbalized and Token Confidence

A language model can state its confidence in words or numbers (Lin et al., 2022a; Mielke et al., 2022). It can give a probability together with its answer (Tian et al., 2023), or rate a proposed answer, as in P(True) (Kadavath et al., 2022). Token confidence instead reads the probability that the model assigns to an answer, as a single-token probability, a sequence likelihood, a length-normalized likelihood, or an inverse perplexity (Desai and Durrett, 2020; Lyu et al., 2024; Huang et al., 2024; Khanmohammadi et al., 2025). Studies that compare the two reach different conclusions. Tian et al. (2023) find that verbalized scores are better calibrated than sampled conditional probabilities, whereas Ni et al. (2024) find token confidence better for less common questions and Xiong et al. (2024) find agreement among sampled answers better than verbalized confidence. We show that which signal looks better can change with how the comparison is measured, even for the same answers.

2.2 Sensitivity of Confidence Scores to Measurement

Both signals depend on how they are measured. Verbalized confidence changes with the prompt (Xiong et al., 2024; Yang et al., 2024) and the response scale (Dai and Wang, 2026), and token confidence with how token probabilities are combined (Yang et al., 2024). ECE (§3.5) changes with its estimator (Nixon et al., 2019; Błasiok and Nakkiran, 2024), and ECE alone can mislead when methods are compared (Müller et al., 2026; Wu et al., 2026). Studies that change the prompt usually also change the answer being scored.

2.3 Scoring Context and Rated Answer

In this study, we change where the token score is read while keeping the question, the answer, and its label the same. The closest design is that of Xia et al. (2026), who score the same answer under several formulations of the task prompt, but not in contexts that differ in whether they ask for confidence. Prior work differs in where it reads the token score. Huang et al. (2024) and Kumar et al. (2024) read it under the prompt that produced the answer, whereas Ni et al. (2024) and Tao et al. (2025) read it under a prompt that also asks for confidence. Others, such as Lyu et al. (2024), do not say where (Appendix J).

Verbalized confidence also depends on which answer the model rates. A chat model is more confident in its own answer than in the same answer attributed to the user (Sanz-Guerrero et al., 2026), and its stated confidence can be largely independent of the answer (Seo et al., 2026). Our supplied-answer probe shows related patterns without attributing answers to anyone (§4.5).

3 Method

Comparing verbalized and token confidence requires several choices, and each can change the result. We first define what both scores must describe and list the choices, then describe our setup.

3.1 Confidence Scores and Alignment

A confidence score expresses how likely a model’s answer a^i\hat{a}_{i} to a question qiq_{i} is correct. We compare two such scores for the same answer. The verbalized score cverb,ic_{\mathrm{verb},i} is the probability that the model states for a^i\hat{a}_{i}. The token score ctok,ic_{\mathrm{tok},i} is instead read from the model’s output distribution. It is the geometric mean of the probabilities that the model assigns to the tokens of a^i\hat{a}_{i} after some input text (forced decoding), so it does not depend on the answer’s length. Both scores are evaluated against the correctness label yiy_{i}, which records whether a^i\hat{a}_{i} is correct.

Alignment rule.

The verbalized score, the token score, and the correctness label must all refer to the same model answer to the same question. Scoring the reference answer instead of the model’s own answer breaks this rule (§4.2 reports what it changes).

3.2 Protocol Choices

We study how the measurement protocol changes the measured confidence of a model, and the comparison between its two confidence signals. A protocol is a full set of choices, and we call each choice an axis. Table 1 lists the axes we vary.

The most important axis is the scoring context. The scoring context, or context for short, is the text placed before the answer when the token score is read, and the answer slot is where the answer starts. The answer was generated in only one context. In every other context, the token score describes an answer the model did not produce there.

3.3 Models and Data

We use five open instruction-tuned models from three developers: Llama-3-8B-Instruct (Meta AI, 2024), Mistral-7B-Instruct-v0.3 (Jiang et al., 2023), Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct (Qwen Team, 2024), Qwen3.5-9B (Qwen Team, 2026) without thinking mode, and Ministral-3-8B-Instruct (Mistral AI, 2025), each with its released chat template. We use TriviaQA (Joshi et al., 2017), SciQ (Welbl et al., 2017), TruthfulQA (Lin et al., 2022b), and MMLU (Hendrycks et al., 2021) with four subjects, which gives five models ×\times four datasets == 20 settings, each with 734 to 1,155 items. Answers use greedy decoding, and we drop unparsed rows; the lowest parse rate is .898.898. We also repeat the main analysis on larger models (Qwen2.5-14B, 32B, and 72B, and Ministral-3-14B) and on the base versions of the five models. Details are in Appendix A. We release code, prompts, labels, and outputs.

3.4 Contexts and Correctness

Contexts.

We fix each model’s answer and its verbalized score, and read the token score of the same answer in three contexts (Figure 2). Both the answer and the verbalized score come from one generation under the confidence prompt of Tian et al. (2023). The prompt asks for “your best guess and the probability that it is correct (0.0 to 1.0)”, with only these two as output: the guess, written after Guess:, is the model’s answer a^i\hat{a}_{i}, and the probability, written after Probability:, is how likely the model says that guess is correct, which is the verbalized score. Each model’s chat template splits the input into a user turn, which holds the prompt, and an assistant turn, where the model writes its reply. The three contexts differ in the text before a^i\hat{a}_{i}:

  • •

    Bare context: the user turn is the question followed by Answer:; a^i\hat{a}_{i} starts the assistant turn.

  • •

    Answer: slot: the user turn is the question alone; the assistant turn starts with Answer:, followed by a^i\hat{a}_{i}.

  • •

    Guess: slot: the user turn is the confidence prompt; the assistant turn starts with Guess:, followed by a^i\hat{a}_{i}. This is where the model generated a^i\hat{a}_{i}.

The first two contexts differ only in where the turn-switch tokens of the chat template fall relative to Answer: and, as a result, in whether the answer starts with a space. The third also changes the instruction, the marker, and the generation context.

Prompt ablation.

The Answer: slot and the Guess: slot differ in both the user prompt and the marker. To see which of the two moves the gap, we cross four user prompts with the markers Answer: and Guess:. The prompts add the parts of the confidence prompt one at a time: the question alone; an answer-only instruction, which asks only for a short guess; the confidence prompt without its probability request; and the full confidence prompt. We call the answer-only instruction with Answer: the answer-only context (Appendix C).

Answers from another prompt.

In the bare context and the Answer: slot, the token score describes an answer that the model generated under another prompt. To test whether this matters, we compare answers to the same question that come from two prompts. Besides the answers a^i\hat{a}_{i} from the confidence prompt, we also ask each model the question under the answer-only instruction, which gives a second set of answers b^i\hat{b}_{i}. We score both sets in the same contexts, on the items that have both.

Correctness.

The correctness label yiy_{i} depends on the correctness rule that grades the answer. Our default is normalized containment: after normalization, the answer equals a gold answer or one of the two strings contains the other (Appendix A). We also use exact match and a multiple-choice format, in which the model sees the options of SciQ and MMLU and answers with a letter (Appendix F).

3.5 Metrics

We use three metrics, defined in Appendix A. ECE (expected calibration error) is the average difference between confidence and accuracy over confidence bins, 10 equal-width bins by default. AUROC is the probability that a correct answer receives higher confidence than a wrong one. AURC is the average error when answers are kept in order of confidence. ECE reads a score as a probability of correctness, which the token score need not be. AUROC and AURC use only the ranking of scores, so they do not depend on their scale.

For context XX, the gap

gXM=M⁡(cverb,y)−M⁡(ctokX,y)g^{M}_{X}=M(c_{\mathrm{verb}},y)-M(c^{X}_{\mathrm{tok}},y)

compares the two signals on the same answers, where MM is a metric and XX is the context in which the token score is read. We write gbareg_{\mathrm{bare}}, gAnswer:g_{\texttt{Answer:}}, and gGuess:g_{\texttt{Guess:}} for the three contexts. The sign of gg depends on the metric. For ECE and AURC, lower is better, so g>0g>0 means the token score is better. For AUROC, higher is better, so g>0g>0 means the verbalized score is better. The context shift is Δg=gGuess:−gbare\Delta g=g_{\texttt{Guess:}}-g_{\mathrm{bare}}.

We measure the size of the shift by the mean |Δ​g||\Delta g| over the 20 settings, and its consistency by the number of settings whose 95% paired bootstrap interval of Δ​g\Delta g excludes zero. We also count flips, settings where the better signal differs between the bare context and the Guess: slot. A flip judged by point estimates may reflect noise, so we call a flip fully resolved when the 95% intervals of gg in both contexts exclude zero, and we give the point-estimate count in parentheses. Because flips also depend on how close the two signals are, we treat them as secondary to the shift itself.

3.6 Supplied Answers

The main comparison always rates the model’s own answer, so the source of the rated answer is not a protocol axis. We still vary it, to check how sensitive and reliable the verbalized score is. We ask whether it depends on how a correct answer is written, whether it separates right from wrong answers, and whether it favors the model’s own answers.

We place a supplied answer after Guess: and let the model write only the probability. The supplied answer is the canonical reference (the dataset’s reference answer) or a plausible wrong answer (another model’s wrong answer to the same question). When no other model answered the question wrongly, we supply an off-type answer instead (the reference answer of another question), only as a check that confidence can drop. The model is not told who wrote a supplied answer. Re-supplying the model’s own answer changes its confidence by at most .022.022 in any setting. On TriviaQA, which lists several accepted spellings of an answer, we also supply two correct forms of the same answer, the first listed alias and the canonical reference, and compare the confidence they receive (Appendix I).

4 Results

4.1 Context Shift

Changing the scoring context from the bare context to the Guess: slot moves the gap about as much as the gap itself (Table 2). Averaged over the 20 settings (§3.3), the gap shifts by .287.287 under ECE, and the bare-context gap is .304.304. Under AUROC, the two numbers are .189.189 and .145.145. For comparison, switching the ECE estimator moves the gap by only .005.005 to .027.027 (§4.4). The shift is rarely noise, since its interval excludes zero in 19 of 20 settings under ECE and in 17 under AUROC (Figure 3).

Under AUROC, the shift always goes the same way: in all 20 settings, the token score ranks the answers better in the Guess: slot. Its AUROC rises from .568.568 to .757.757 on average, while the verbalized score stays at .702.702. AUROC depends only on the order of the scores, so rescaling alone cannot change it. The rise means that the context changes the order of the answers.

Under ECE, the shift has no fixed direction. The context also changes the level of the token score: its mean rises from .149.149 in the bare context to .732.732 in the Guess: slot. In the bare context, the token score is underconfident: its mean is below accuracy in 18 settings. In the Guess: slot, it is overconfident: its mean is above accuracy in all 20. So in which context the token score is better calibrated depends on the accuracy. When accuracy is above .5.5, the token score is better calibrated in the Guess: slot in 8 of 10 settings. When accuracy is below .5.5, it never is.

The shift often flips which signal looks better (§3.5). Under ECE, the better signal flips in 8 settings, and all 8 flips are fully resolved. Under AUROC, 8 flips are fully resolved, and 5 more appear only in the point estimates.

The shift also appears when the model states its confidence on a 0–100 scale instead of 0.0–1.0 (Appendix B.1). It appears in larger models as well (Appendix B.2), and under exact match, a stricter correctness rule (§4.3). It is weaker in base models, where its interval excludes zero in 11 settings under ECE and 12 under AUROC (Appendix B.3).

4.2 Prompt Ablation and Baseline Choice

The gap moves mainly when the instruction changes, and little when Answer: moves (Table 3). Moving Answer: into the assistant turn changes the AUROC gap only from +.134+.134 to +.153+.153. Replacing the plain question with the answer-only instruction turns it negative, to −.019-.019. The full confidence prompt then moves it a little further, to −.055-.055. The ECE gap moves by .031.031 on average when Answer: moves, but by .175.175 when the instruction changes (Appendix C).

Which prompt serves as the baseline matters even among prompts that do not ask for confidence. The Answer: slot and the answer-only context both use such prompts, yet the better signal differs between them in 4 settings under ECE and 3 under AUROC (fully resolved flips). The shift to the Guess: slot also depends on this choice. From the bare context, it is .287.287 under ECE and .189.189 under AUROC (§4.1). From the answer-only context, it is only .113.113 and .050.050, with no fully resolved flip.

In the bare context, the token score hardly favors answers from either prompt. In the Guess: slot, it favors the answer generated there. For each question, we compare two answers from the same model: one generated under the confidence prompt and one generated under the answer-only instruction. In the bare context, the two answers get almost the same token score (they differ by .008.008 on average). In the Guess: slot, the answer generated there gets a token score .187.187 higher (Appendix D).

The reference answer shows the same pattern. Scoring it instead of the model’s answer breaks the alignment rule (§3.1). In the Guess: slot, this lowers the token score by .458.458 on average and moves the ECE gap by .224.224. In the bare context, the two changes are only .048.048 and .054.054 (Appendix E).

4.3 Correctness Rule and Answer Format

The correctness rule moves the gap mainly in the bare context and under ECE. We leave out TruthfulQA, where exact-match accuracy is below .05.05, and use the other 15 settings. Switching from the default rule to exact match changes the ECE gap by .181.181 in the bare context but by only .005.005 in the Guess: slot (Table 4). Under AUROC, the two changes are .033.033 and .027.027.

The bare context and the Guess: slot differ because the token score lies on different sides of accuracy in the two (§4.1). ECE measures how far a score is from accuracy. Under exact match, accuracy is .106.106 lower on average. In the bare context, the token score is below accuracy in 14 of the 15 settings, and the verbalized score is above it in all 15. When accuracy drops, it gets closer to the token score and further from the verbalized score. As a result, the gap moves in favor of the token score in all 15 settings. In the Guess: slot, both scores are above accuracy, so lower accuracy moves away from both, and the gap barely changes.

The context shift itself remains large under exact match. Over the same 15 settings, the mean |Δ​g||\Delta g| is .237.237 under ECE and .235.235 under AUROC, compared with .283.283 and .210.210 under the default rule. By point estimate, flips go from 8 to 5 under ECE and from 10 to 11 under AUROC.

SciQ and MMLU are multiple-choice datasets, but our main setup asks the model to answer in free text. In the multiple-choice format, the model instead sees the options and answers with a letter, and the bare context already asks for a letter only, like the answer-only context (§4.2). In this format, the size of the ECE shift depends on the model. It stays large for Qwen3.5-9B (.148.148 and .343.343) but is .057.057 or less for the other models. Under AUROC, the shift averages .043.043, and the better signal never flips (Appendix F).

4.4 Comparing the Axes

The context moves the gap more than any other axis, and the estimator moves it least (Table 4). Under ECE, with the token score read in the bare context, the order is the context (.287.287), the correctness rule (.181.181), token aggregation (.054.054), and the estimator (.027.027 or less; Appendix G). The order changes with where the token score is read. In the Guess: slot, the correctness rule moves the ECE gap by only .005.005, less than token aggregation does (.060.060; §4.3).

Even two axes together allow a wide range of gaps. Across the six protocols that combine the three contexts with the two aggregations, the largest point estimate of gg exceeds the smallest by .336.336 under ECE and .230.230 under AUROC on average (Appendix H). Both ranges are larger than the bare-context gap itself (.304.304 and .145.145).

4.5 Supplied Answers

The main comparison rates the model’s own answer. Here we fix the rated answer ourselves and look at what the stated confidence responds to (§3.6). These results concern the level of verbalized confidence, not the gap.

Stated confidence changes with how a correct answer is written. On TriviaQA, supplying the canonical reference instead of the first listed alias raises confidence by .114.114 ([.105,.123][.105,.123]), although both are correct. The rise is limited to items where the two strings differ (.152.152); where they are the same, the difference is −.002-.002. The canonical form is also closer to how the models answer: it matches the model’s own correct answer in 77%77\% of cases, against 18%18\% for the first alias.

Stated confidence separates a right answer from a plausible wrong one only weakly. The canonical reference gets .056.056 ([.050,.062][.050,.062]) more confidence than another model’s wrong answer to the same question. It gets less in 22%22\% of pairs and the same in 46%46\%. When the plausible wrong answer is also a wrong option listed by the benchmark, the margin is .083.083 ([.045,.121][.045,.121]). As a sanity check, off-type answers get .183.183 on average.

On questions the model got wrong, stated confidence leans toward the model’s own answer. Its wrong answer gets .044.044 ([.037,.050][.037,.050]) more confidence than another model’s wrong answer to the same question, and about as much as the canonical reference (a difference of .008.008). When the model’s answer is correct but written differently from the canonical reference, the two get about the same confidence (.005.005, [−.002,.012][-.002,.012]). The lean resembles the self-preference of LLM evaluators, which score their own outputs higher than others’ (Panickssery et al., 2024). Our model is not told who wrote a supplied answer, so the lean may reflect agreement with its own belief rather than authorship, much as Wataoka et al. (2024) link self-preference to how familiar a text is to the model (Appendix I).

4.6 Implications for Reporting

The gap between verbalized and token confidence depends on the protocol as well as on the two signals. Table 5 turns our results into reporting items. Each item changed the gap, the verbalized score, or the number of flips in our experiments, or is a rule whose violation did. ECE compares a score with accuracy, so its verdict depends on accuracy, while AUROC does not (§4.1); a report should therefore give both.

No context is a neutral token baseline, so the choice should follow the use of the score and be reported. If a model scores its own answer to decide whether to give it, the token score should be read in the prompt that produced the answer. That is the context in use, and there the token score ranks the answers better than in the bare context (Table 2; Appendix D.1). If the score checks an answer from elsewhere, its token score is lower than for an answer generated in the same context (§4.2), so a threshold set on the model’s own answers does not carry over. The verbalized score also separates right from wrong supplied answers only weakly and depends on their wording (§4.5). Such a check should be calibrated on answers from the same source.

Confidence used for abstention needs the same care. The token score changes level between contexts, from .149.149 to .732.732 on average (§4.1), and a calibration map fitted in one context does not carry over to the other (Appendix G). A threshold should be set in the context where the score is used.

5 Conclusion

LLM confidence is sensitive to the protocol used to measure it. Even with the answer and its label fixed, the context in which the token score is read shifts the gap between verbalized and token confidence by about its own size and changes how the token score ranks the answers. Within that context, the instruction matters more than where the answer begins. Other choices, such as the correctness rule and token aggregation, can also change which score looks better. Stated confidence also depends on how the rated answer is written. Reports of LLM confidence and comparisons of calibration should therefore fix and report the measurement protocol first. Table 5 lists what to report. In practice, confidence scores should be checked under the prompt in which they are used.

Limitations

Our experiments cover English short-answer QA with open 7–9B models, with larger and base models as checks. Closed models, long-form answers, multi-turn dialogue, and reasoning before the answer remain to be tested. We use greedy decoding, one verbalized prompt with a 0–100 variant, and string-matching correctness rather than human grading.

Our design scores a fixed answer in contexts that did not all produce it. It isolates the score of one answer rather than comparing two prompting systems end to end, and the transfer check with answer-only answers tests whether the shift carries over, not a causal effect of where an answer comes from. The prompt ablation reports changes from text edits along stated paths, so we do not attribute the shift to any single prompt element. The review of published comparisons includes only studies that compare both signals and state a conclusion; it shows that conventions differ, not how common each is. Finally, intervals are not corrected for multiple comparisons, and we report flips, which depend on intervals near zero, after the size of the shift.

Ethical Considerations

We study released open models on public QA benchmarks. We do not train or deploy models, collect user data, or involve human participants, and we release our code, prompts, labels, and model outputs. The benchmarks may contain outdated facts or offensive content; we use them only for aggregate evaluation.

The main risk this work points to is misplaced trust in a confidence score. Systems that abstain, escalate, or verify answers based on confidence inherit the protocol under which that confidence was measured, and a threshold or calibration set under one prompt may not hold under another (§4.6). A favorable comparison reported without its protocol could encourage such misuse in high-stakes settings. We therefore recommend reporting the protocol and validating confidence under the deployed prompt, rather than treating either score as a general measure of reliability.

Appendix A Reproducibility Details

Models.

Table 6 lists the checkpoints. The main analysis uses the instruction-tuned checkpoints. We also repeat it on the base checkpoints and on four larger instruction-tuned models.

Data.

Table 7 lists the data sources, and Table 8 the number of items per setting after we drop unparsed rows.

Licenses and content.

SciQ is released under CC BY-NC 3.0, TruthfulQA under Apache-2.0, MMLU under MIT, and the TriviaQA repository under Apache-2.0. We use the models under their released licenses: Apache-2.0 for all except Llama-3-8B (Llama 3 Community License) and Qwen2.5-72B (Qwen License). All are used for research evaluation, which these terms allow. Our released outputs contain the benchmark questions, so they inherit these terms; in particular, the SciQ records are for non-commercial use only. The benchmarks are public and contain no data about private individuals, and we add none. We do not filter questions or outputs for content. The model outputs, including the supplied wrong answers, may contain false or objectionable statements; the release documents this and is intended only for reproducing our measurements.

Generation.

Answers use greedy decoding with at most 32 new tokens. We keep each checkpoint’s released generation configuration with sampling turned off; for the Qwen2.5 models, this keeps a repetition penalty of 1.05. Main answers are generated one question at a time. The answer-only answers are generated in batches of 16 with left padding for Llama-3-8B, Mistral-7B-v0.3, and Qwen2.5-7B, and one at a time for Qwen3.5-9B and Ministral-3-8B; the multiple-choice answers follow the same rule. Token scores are computed in batches of 16, except for Qwen3.5-9B, whose scores change with padding, and for Ministral-3-8B in the multiple-choice format and on the answer-only answers; these we score one input at a time. Models run in float16, except Qwen2.5-72B, which runs in bfloat16.

Chat templates.

We wrap each prompt as a user turn with the model’s released chat template and let the template open the assistant turn. The Llama-3 and Mistral-7B templates add no system prompt. The Qwen2.5 templates add the default system prompt “You are Qwen, created by Alibaba Cloud. You are a helpful assistant.”, and the Ministral-3 templates add their long default system prompt, whose date placeholder stays unfilled; we keep both. Qwen3.5-9B runs with thinking turned off, so its assistant turn opens with an empty thinking block before the marker or the answer. We load the Ministral-3 tokenizer as released, without the optional fix to its pre-tokenization pattern; the fix does not change the tokens of our inputs.

Prompts and contexts.

Table 9 gives the prompts. In the bare context, the user turn is the bare prompt and the answer starts the assistant turn. In the Answer: slot and the answer-only context, the final Answer: of the bare prompt or of the answer-only instruction moves from the user turn to the start of the assistant turn. In the Guess: slot, the user turn is the confidence prompt and the assistant turn starts with Guess:. In the bare context, the answer starts the assistant turn without a leading space. After Answer: or Guess:, it follows a single space, so the first token of the answer can differ between the bare context and the Answer: slot. We tokenize the context and the parsed answer string separately and join the tokens, so the token score is computed on the parsed answer, not on the generated tokens. The answer-only answers (§3.4) are generated with the full answer-only instruction as the user turn.

Parsing.

The answer is the first non-empty text after a Guess: label; without that label, it is the first line that is not a label. The verbalized score is the number after a Probability: label; if no label matches, the parser takes the first standalone number between 0 and 1 in the output. We drop rows where either is missing. The fallback sets the score of 331 of the 19,604 scored rows, mostly for Ministral-3-8B, which often writes the probability in bold, and Llama-3-8B, which sometimes leaves out the labels. Dropping these rows leaves the main result unchanged: the mean |Δ​g||\Delta g| is .288.288 under ECE and .188.188 under AUROC, with 8 and 13 flips by point estimate. We do not strip Markdown from answers, so 342 of the 3,837 scored answers of Ministral-3-8B keep their asterisks. The lowest parse rate, .898.898, is for Ministral-3-8B on TruthfulQA, where long answers often reach the 32-token limit before the probability line.

Metrics.

ECE sorts the nn answers into 10 equal-width confidence bins and sums, over bins bb, nbn​|accb−confb|\frac{n_{b}}{n}\,|\mathrm{acc}_{b}-\mathrm{conf}_{b}|, where nbn_{b} is the bin size and accb\mathrm{acc}_{b} and confb\mathrm{conf}_{b} are the mean correctness and the mean confidence in the bin. The bins are [k/10,(k+1)/10)[k/10,(k+1)/10), and the last one also includes 1. AUROC is the probability that a randomly chosen correct answer receives higher confidence than a randomly chosen wrong one; ties count one half. For AURC, we keep the kk most confident answers for each k=1,…,nk=1,\dots,n, compute the error rate among them, and average over kk. Answers with tied confidence are ordered at random, and we use the expected value over that ordering.

Normalization.

Normalization lowercases the text, replaces every character other than an ASCII letter, digit, or whitespace with a space, and merges repeated whitespace.

Intervals.

All intervals are 95% percentile intervals from a paired bootstrap with 10,000 resamples. Within a setting, we resample answers and recompute every score on the same resample. Each setting has its own random seed, fixed by its model and dataset. For a mean over settings, we average the resampled values across settings and take the percentiles of that average.

Environment.

We run on NVIDIA A100 80GB GPUs with PyTorch 2.5.1 and Transformers 5.8.1. The checkpoint revisions are the Hugging Face commits listed in Table 6.

Appendix B Further Checks of the Context Shift

Table 10 repeats the main comparison under three changes: a 0–100 confidence scale, larger models, and base checkpoints. Each row uses the same metrics and intervals as Table 2, and the same contexts except where Appendix B.3 notes otherwise.

B.1 Integer 0–100 Elicitation

Here the confidence prompt asks for an integer percentage from 0 to 100 (Table 9), and the Guess: slot uses this prompt. We keep only outputs that contain the Probability: label, which leaves 16,328 of the 19,320 parsed rows (.845.845). Llama-3-8B often leaves out the label, so only .259.259 of its rows remain; each other model keeps at least .991.991. The shift stays about as large as in the main comparison, and token AUROC again rises in the Guess: slot in all 20 settings.

B.2 Larger Models

We run three larger Qwen2.5 models and Ministral-3-14B on the four datasets. To limit compute, Qwen2.5-72B answers only the first 250 questions of TriviaQA, SciQ, and TruthfulQA. In every setting of every larger model, the interval of Δ​g\Delta g excludes zero under both metrics, and token AUROC rises in the Guess: slot. The mean |Δ​g||\Delta g| is at least as large as in the main comparison.

B.3 Base Checkpoints

Base checkpoints often ignore the requested format, so many rows drop out. Of the 3,972 questions per model, we keep .158.158 for Llama-3-8B, .369.369 for Mistral-7B-v0.3, .930.930 for Qwen2.5-7B, .971.971 for Qwen3.5-9B, and .119.119 for Ministral-3-8B. The tokenizers of the two Qwen base models have a chat template, and we use it. The other three have none, so the prompt and the answer form one plain text, and the Answer: slot is the same as the bare context. For these three models, the Guess: slot is the confidence prompt followed by a new line and Guess:, the answer in the bare context also follows a space, and answers are generated without the tokenizer’s beginning-of-sequence token but scored with it. The shift is smaller in base checkpoints, and its direction under AUROC is mixed: token AUROC rises in the Guess: slot in 9 of the 20 settings.

Appendix C Prompt Ablation

Design.

The Answer: slot and the Guess: slot differ in both the user prompt and the marker. We cross four user prompts with the two markers Answer: and Guess: at the start of the assistant turn, and score each model’s main answers in all eight cells. The four prompts are the question alone (the bare prompt without its final Answer:), the answer-only instruction (also without its final Answer:), the confidence prompt without its probability request, and the full confidence prompt (Table 9). To remove the probability request, we delete its three mentions: “and the probability that it is correct (0.0 to 1.0)”, “and probability”, and the Probability: line of the example. Three cells are contexts of the main text: (question, Answer:) is the Answer: slot, (answer-only instruction, Answer:) is the answer-only context, and (confidence prompt, Guess:) is the Guess: slot. Re-scoring the Answer: slot and the Guess: slot for the main answers, and the answer-only context for the answer-only answers, reproduces the stored token scores exactly.

Results.

Table 11 shows where token AUROC changes. Replacing the question with the answer-only instruction raises it in both columns. The marker matters with the question alone (.549.549 to .611.611) but hardly with the answer-only instruction (.722.722 to .719.719). The full step, from the Answer: slot to the Guess: slot, raises token AUROC by .208.208 ([.198,.218][.198,.218]). Along the Guess: path, switching the marker under the question alone adds .062.062 ([.056,.067][.056,.067]), the answer-only instruction .109.109 ([.100,.117][.100,.117]), the rest of the output template .040.040 ([.035,.045][.035,.045]), and the probability request −.002-.002 ([−.007,.004][-.007,.004]). Swapping the marker under the answer-only instruction changes token AUROC by −.003-.003 ([−.005,.000][-.005,.000]). The instruction effect is positive for every model, from .060.060 (Mistral-7B-v0.3) to .225.225 (Qwen2.5-7B).

Order of the edits.

The size of each edit depends on the path. With the Answer: marker fixed, as in Table 3, the answer-only instruction adds .173.173, the output template .020.020, the probability request −.033-.033, and the final switch to Guess: .048.048. We therefore describe each number as the change from one edit along a stated path, not as the share of the shift caused by one part of the prompt.

ECE.

The same edits move the ECE gap by different amounts. On the Guess: path, the mean |Δ​g||\Delta g| is .070.070 for the marker under the question alone, .181.181 for the answer-only instruction, .053.053 for the output template, .060.060 for the probability request, and .020.020 for the marker under the answer-only instruction, against .266.266 for the full step from the Answer: slot to the Guess: slot. On the Answer: path, the probability request moves it by .039.039, the answer-only instruction by .175.175, and the move from the bare context to the Answer: slot by .031.031; these are the values in §4.2. So the probability request leaves the ranking almost unchanged but does shift the level of the token score.

Answers from the answer-only instruction.

We repeat the grid with the answer-only answers (§3.4). The pattern is similar: the answer-only instruction raises token AUROC by .135.135 ([.127,.144][.127,.144]), the probability request changes it by −.002-.002 ([−.007,.003][-.007,.003]), and the marker under the answer-only instruction by −.011-.011 ([−.014,−.007][-.014,-.007]). These answers were generated under the answer-only instruction, so for them this edit also moves the context toward the prompt that produced them.

Selection.

Each answer gets a higher token score in the context where greedy decoding chose it. We take the questions where the main answer and the answer-only answer differ (.595.595 of matched questions) and compare their mean token scores. The main answer scores .121.121 lower in the answer-only context and .318.318 higher in the Guess: slot, where it was produced. The answer-only context uses the instruction that produced the answer-only answer but differs from its generating context in where Answer: falls. The difference between the two contexts, .438.438 ([.431,.445][.431,.445]), ranges from .293.293 to .611.611 across models.

Appendix D Answers from Another Prompt

In the bare context and the Answer: slot, the token score describes an answer that the model generated under another prompt. To see whether this matters, we use two answers from the same model to each question: the main answer a^i\hat{a}_{i} from the confidence prompt and the answer-only answer b^i\hat{b}_{i} from the answer-only instruction (Table 9). We read the token score of both answers in the bare context and in the Guess: slot. An average setting has 980 questions with both answers, and the two answers differ on .595.595 of them (exact string match). When the two strings are the same, their token scores differ by at most .010.010; this comes from batched scoring, and Qwen3.5-9B, scored one input at a time, shows no difference.

Table 12 shows the result. In the bare context, the main answer scores slightly lower than the answer-only answer (−.008-.008). In the Guess: slot, where the main answer was generated, it scores .187.187 higher. The difference between the two contexts is .195.195 ([.191,.199][.191,.199]) and ranges from .143.143 to .255.255 across models. So the bare context scores the two answers alike, although neither was generated there, while the Guess: slot favors the answer generated there.

D.1 Transfer Check

We also repeat the main comparison with the answer-only answers in place of the main answers. Each answer-only answer keeps its own correctness label. Its verbalized score comes from supplying it after Guess:, with the same format as in §3.6, because the answer-only instruction does not ask for a probability. We read its token score in three contexts: the bare context, the prompt that generated it, and the Guess: slot.

The shift from the bare context to the Guess: slot remains. Its mean |Δ​g||\Delta g| is .181.181 under ECE and .161.161 under AUROC, and its interval excludes zero in 17 and 15 of 20 settings. The better signal flips in 6 settings under ECE and 4 under AUROC (7 and 10 by point estimate). For these answers, token AUROC is highest in the prompt that generated them (.775.775), against .730.730 in the Guess: slot and .573.573 in the bare context; the verbalized AUROC is .708.708. Because the verbalized score here rates a supplied answer, this check tests whether the shift carries over to other answers, not the main comparison itself.

Appendix E Scoring the Reference String

A token baseline breaks the alignment rule (§3.1) if it scores the reference answer instead of the model’s answer. To measure what this changes, we read the token score of the canonical reference (Appendix I) in the three contexts and keep the verbalized score and the label of the model’s answer. The reference is the same string as the model’s answer, ignoring case, for .265.265 of the answers.

Table 13 shows two effects. First, the reference gets a lower token score than the model’s answer in every context, and by far the most in the Guess: slot (.732.732 to .273.273), where the model generated its answer. So under ECE, the substitution moves the gap most in that slot (.224.224, against .054.054 in the bare context). This ECE compares a score for one string with a label for another, so it is not a calibration result for either answer.

Second, the reference often ranks the model’s answers better than the answers themselves do. Mean token AUROC is higher in every context, and it is higher in 16, 16, and 12 of the 20 settings in the three contexts. The reference separates right from wrong answers more sharply. In the Guess: slot, it gets .460.460 on average when the model’s answer is correct and .105.105 when it is wrong, while the model’s own answer gets .833.833 and .658.658. The substitution thus makes the token score look better, and under AUROC the better signal flips in 4 to 7 of the 20 settings.

Appendix F Correctness Rule and Answer Format

Exact match.

Under exact match, the answer must equal a gold answer after normalization (Appendix A). We leave TruthfulQA out of exact-match summaries, because its exact-match accuracy is .023.023 to .048.048 across models. Over the other 15 settings, exact match lowers accuracy from .493.493 to .387.387 on average. This raises the bare-context ECE gap in all 15 settings, by .181.181 on average and by at least .039.039, while the Guess: gap moves by only .005.005 (§4.3). The context shift stays large: its mean |Δ​g||\Delta g| goes from .283.283 to .237.237 under ECE and from .210.210 to .235.235 under AUROC. By point estimate, ECE flips fall from 8 to 5 and AUROC flips go from 10 to 11. The three ECE flips that disappear are all on SciQ (Llama-3-8B, Ministral-3-8B, and Qwen2.5-7B), where the bare gap was negative and becomes positive, like the Guess: gap.

Multiple-choice format.

SciQ and MMLU are multiple-choice datasets. In this format, the model sees four lettered options and answers with a letter, which is correct if it matches the gold letter. For SciQ, the options are the correct answer and the three listed distractors in a shuffled order; for MMLU, they are the four given choices. This format uses its own two prompts (Table 9). The multiple-choice confidence prompt asks for the option letter and its probability, and the Guess: slot uses it. The letter-only prompt asks for one option letter without a probability; the bare context uses it, and the Answer: slot adds Answer: at the start of the assistant turn. The model writes at most 20 new tokens, and the SciQ options are shuffled with a fixed seed for each question. Unlike the bare prompt of the main analysis, this prompt contains an answer-only instruction, so it is closer to the answer-only context of §4.2.

Table 14 gives the results. Accuracy is high, from .646.646 to .964.964. The ECE shift is small for four models and large for Qwen3.5-9B, so its mean over the 10 settings is .071.071, and .027.027 without Qwen3.5-9B. Its interval excludes zero in 7 settings under ECE and 5 under AUROC. Under ECE, the better signal flips in 1 setting (5 by point estimate). Under AUROC and AURC, it flips in none.

Appendix G Estimators, Bin Counts, and Calibration Transfer

Estimators.

Besides 10-bin ECE, we use three estimators without fixed bins. KDE is a plain kernel estimate in the spirit of Zhang et al. (2020), not their exact estimator: it estimates accuracy at each answer’s confidence by Gaussian kernel regression (bandwidth .05.05) and averages its absolute difference from the confidence over answers. KS follows Gupta et al. (2021): it sorts answers by confidence and takes the largest absolute cumulative difference between correctness and confidence, divided by nn. Smoothed follows Błasiok and Nakkiran (2024) in smoothing both the accuracy curve and the confidence density with a Gaussian kernel, but uses a plain kernel with Silverman’s bandwidth instead of their reflected kernel and bandwidth rule.

Table 15 gives the results. Changing the estimator moves the gap by .027.027 or less on average. The largest change in a single setting is .092.092 (KS, bare context). Only one estimator changes the better signal in one setting (Smoothed, Guess: slot, Mistral-7B-v0.3 on TruthfulQA). The context flips stay at 8 or 9 under every estimator.

Bin counts.

With 5, 10, 15, 20, 30, or 50 equal-width bins, the better signal flips between the bare context and the Guess: slot in 8 settings, and between the Answer: slot and the Guess: slot in 7 settings, at every bin count (point estimates).

Calibration transfer.

Recalibrating the token score within one context removes any monotone difference in its scale. The recalibrated scores still differ between contexts. With isotonic regression fitted and evaluated in the same context, the Brier score is .196.196 in the bare context and .170.170 in the Guess: slot (.200.200 and .170.170 with Platt scaling). A calibration map also does not carry over between contexts. We fit the map on the token scores of one context and apply it to the token scores of the same answers in the other context, cross-fitting with 5 folds and repeating with 10 random splits. The penalty is the Brier score of the transferred map minus that of a map fitted in the same context. It is positive in all 20 settings, for both methods and both directions, and in every repeat. On average it is .124.124 (isotonic) and .128.128 (Platt) when a map from the Guess: slot is applied to the bare context, and .149.149 and .049.049 in the other direction.

Appendix H Protocol Ranges

A reader who reimplements a comparison without the protocol has to pick one. To see how much the pick can matter, we take each setting, compute the gap gg under every protocol in a set, and record two numbers: the width (the largest minus the smallest point estimate of gg) and whether the protocols give both signs. Table 16 reports the mean width over the 20 settings and the number of settings with both signs.

The range grows as we add axes. With the three contexts and the two aggregations, the width is .336.336 under ECE and .230.230 under AUROC, larger than the bare-context gap itself (.304.304 and .145.145). The sign of the comparison differs across these six protocols in 9 settings under ECE and 17 under AUROC. Scoring the reference string widens the range further, but such protocols break the alignment rule, so we keep them apart.

These numbers are point estimates, and a large width can partly reflect noise. They are also a lower bound on the range a reader faces, because we vary only the axes in the table.

Appendix I Supplied Answers

Setup.

The user turn is the confidence prompt. We start the assistant turn with Guess:, the supplied answer, a new line, and Probability:, and let the model write at most 12 more tokens. The canonical reference is the answer.value field for TriviaQA and the first gold answer of Table 7 for the other datasets (for TruthfulQA, the best answer). The plausible wrong answer is a wrong answer that another model gave to the same question and that differs from the model’s own answer. The other models available depend on when each model was run: Llama-3-8B, Mistral-7B-v0.3, and Qwen2.5-7B draw on each other, Qwen3.5-9B on these three, and Ministral-3-8B on the other four. When several candidates exist, we take the one from the model whose name comes first alphabetically. When there is none, we supply an off-type answer: the first gold answer of a random other question, checked to be wrong for this one. Off-type answers therefore go to questions where no other model gave a different wrong answer, mostly questions that the other models answered correctly. On these questions the model’s own accuracy is .765.765, against .236.236 on questions with a plausible wrong answer. A looser normalization (ignoring case, accents, and plural endings) flags plausible wrong answers that are close to the reference. We judged the flagged strings by hand, accepted 26 as correct, and removed the 69 pairs that use them, out of 12,609.

Levels.

Averaged over the 20 settings, the model states .913.913 for its own correct answers and .813.813 for its own wrong answers. It states .821.821 for the canonical reference, .761.761 for a plausible wrong answer, and .183.183 for an off-type answer. These levels come from different sets of questions, so Table 17 compares answers to the same questions instead.

Wording.

On TriviaQA, the canonical reference gets more confidence than the first listed alias. The gap comes only from questions where the two strings differ. Over all questions, it ranges from +.030+.030 (Llama-3-8B) to +.225+.225 (Qwen3.5-9B) across models. The canonical form matches the model’s own correct answer in 77%77\% of cases and the first alias in 18%18\%.

Right versus wrong.

The canonical reference beats a plausible wrong answer by +.074+.074 on TriviaQA, +.074+.074 on SciQ, +.076+.076 on TruthfulQA, and +.022+.022 on MMLU. The TriviaQA value depends on the wording of the reference. If we supply the first listed alias instead, the difference on TriviaQA becomes −.019-.019 ([−.036,−.002][-.036,-.002]): the wrong answer gets more confidence than the correct one. On the 412 pairs where the plausible wrong answer is also a wrong option listed by SciQ, TruthfulQA, or MMLU, and so wrong by the benchmark’s own labels, the margin is +.083+.083.

Own versus supplied.

On the questions the model got wrong, its own wrong answer gets about as much confidence as the canonical reference and more than another model’s wrong answer. On the questions it got right, its own answer and a differently written canonical reference get about the same confidence. Re-supplying the model’s own answer changes the mean confidence by at most .022.022 in any setting and leaves .969.969 of the individual values unchanged on average, so starting the assistant turn with a supplied answer changes the stated confidence little.

Appendix J Review of Published Comparisons

This review asks how published comparisons of verbalized and token confidence choose and report the protocol. It is targeted, not a survey: it shows that the choices differ and are sometimes unstated, and it does not estimate how often this happens in the field.

Collection and inclusion.

We collected candidates from web searches of arXiv and the ACL Anthology on verbalized confidence and its comparison with token probabilities, from papers suggested to us during earlier reviewing, and from related work we read during the project. This gave 22 candidates. A study is included if it evaluates a verbalized or self-reported signal and a probabilistic signal tied to one candidate answer, and states a conclusion about their relative performance or their agreement. Twelve studies meet this criterion; Table 18 lists the ten exclusions. Every judgment rests on a quote that we located in the source text, not on a summary of it.

Table 19 includes studies that evaluate both signal types on the same items and state a conclusion about their relative performance or their agreement. Each row is one method of one study; a study has several rows when its methods differ in context or aggregation, so the twelve studies give fifteen rows. S marks an explicit statement, P a choice the paper leaves unstated but whose coarse form follows from the scoring operation the method describes, U no recoverable choice, and – an inapplicable axis. The final column records where the probabilistic-side signal is obtained: G for a prompt that does not ask for confidence and E for one that does, whether jointly with the answer or after an answer is supplied. The nine studies of the first round were rated twice by the same rule, and the second pass changed four judgments, listed after the evidence ledger; the three studies added afterwards were rated once by that rubric.

Table 20 records the source locations used to assign the non-U cells. For context/slot, we searched the methods and prompt appendices for both the conditioning prompt and the answer position. A paper receives S only when both are determined. Code availability means an author-linked implementation of the evaluated method, not merely a model or dataset repository.

Second rating pass.

Because the audit rests on one rater, we derived it a second time. For the nine studies of the first round we re-downloaded every source, re-located every quoted string, and, for the context axis, extracted every sentence mentioning the probabilistic-side signal and read those that also mention a prompt, context, or position. All quoted strings were found again. Four judgments changed: Tao et al. (2025) and Müller et al. (2026) from unspecified to stated, Xia et al. (2026) from unspecified to stated for context and partly determined for aggregation, Lin et al. (2022a) from inapplicable to unspecified for aggregation, and the aggregation evidence for one further study, which had been taken from that paper’s description of a different method. A later refinement of the P category moved the context axis of Lin et al. (2022a), Lyu et al. (2024), and Testoni and Calixto (2026) from unspecified to partly determined, and that of Huang et al. (2024) to stated once we located its generation prompt. The first pass had applied two different questions: whether a reimplementation can determine the probabilistic-side context, and whether the paper says the two signals share one context. The table uses the first question throughout. Ni et al. (2024) and Kumar et al. (2024) were added after that round, and Xiong et al. (2024) after a later re-reading of the inclusion criterion; each was rated by the same rubric in a single pass over its source; for Ni et al. (2024) the context axis was re-derived once more after an initial reading treated the suppressed prompt in its scoring formula as an omission rather than as shorthand.

Source corrections.

A last comparison against the source texts, for the arXiv versions named in the ledger, changed the following. The aggregation of Tao et al. (2025) moved from unspecified to stated, because the introduction describes the inverse perplexity of the generated response. The code of Huang et al. (2024) and Testoni and Calixto (2026) is linked in the abstract and the introduction. The context of Testoni and Calixto (2026) moved from partly determined to stated, because Appendix B gives the generation prompt and how the response begins. Lin et al. (2022a) is split into the answer logit, read on the model’s answer, and the indirect logit, read after an appended true/false query. Müller et al. (2026) is rated on its second experiment, the one that compares verbalized confidence with other signals, with its methods in separate rows. Khanmohammadi et al. (2025) is excluded, because its compared signals all derive from one self-evaluation token probability and it has no verbalized arm in words. These changes were made in a single pass over each source, by the same rubric.

The distinction matters in practice. Tian et al. (2023) use a ten-sample frequency estimate rather than per-token likelihood, so an open-weight reimplementation has no original token score or answer slot to copy. Yang et al. (2024) likewise identify logit aggregation as a design choice, and Xia et al. (2026) note that prompt robustness remains understudied. These points motivate explicit specification; they do not invalidate the cited results.
